# File Viewer — Technical Notes

Companion to `PROBLEM.md`. Records the non-obvious technical decisions made while building v0.1, the traps I hit, and the load-bearing choices future work should not accidentally undo.

Repo: `/Volumes/D/www/projects/khanakia/chrome-extensions/file-viewer`

## Repo shape

```
apps/
  chrome-ext/                MV3 host — Vite + React + Tailwind v4
    public/manifest.json     MV3 manifest (action, service worker, content_scripts, web_accessible_resources)
    src/app/                 Main viewer page (library shell, adapters, registry, intercept pickup)
    src/background/          Service worker (dev reload + icon click → open tab)
    src/content/             file:// interception
    src/styles/              Tailwind v4 + design tokens driven by [data-theme]
packages/
  viewer-core/               @file-viewer/core — types, ThemeProvider, adapter interfaces, memory defaults
  mdx-viewer/                @file-viewer/mdx — the renderer (host-agnostic)
pnpm-workspace.yaml
tsconfig.base.json
```

Workspace root builds viewer packages first (tsup), then the host app (Vite). Each viewer package ships ESM + `.d.ts` and declares React as a peer.

## The MV3 / unsafe-eval collision (most important decision)

**MV3 forbids `'unsafe-eval'` in extension-page CSP.** The default is effectively `script-src 'self'` for any `chrome-extension://` page. Loading a manifest that tries to add `'unsafe-eval'` is rejected by Chrome.

This kills `@mdx-js/mdx`'s `evaluate()` flow, which depends on `new AsyncFunction(compiledCode)` at runtime. Every path that compiles MDX → runtime React component uses eval.

**The available escape hatches:**
1. **Sandboxed pages** (`sandbox` manifest key) — get `'unsafe-eval'` implicitly but lose access to `chrome.*` APIs. Viewer has to live inside an iframe; parent shell communicates via `postMessage`.
2. **No-eval pipeline** — give up MDX JSX expression evaluation. Use `unified → remarkParse → remarkGfm → remarkRehype({allowDangerousHtml}) → rehypeRaw → React` instead. MDX JSX expressions (`{count * 2}`) don't work; HTML-tag components (`<Callout>`) do, because rehype-raw keeps them as tags for react-markdown's components map.

**v0.1 chose option 2.** Reasons: no iframe bridging, no `postMessage` plumbing, no split between "safe remote" and "trusted local" content. The tradeoff: users can't compute values in MDX. In practice for a reading-focused viewer, that's fine — the 99% use case is "pretty rendering + callouts + task lists + math + code". All of those work without eval.

**v0.2+ can add the sandbox-iframe path** as an opt-in renderer for true `.mdx` with JSX expressions. Architecture supports it: add a second renderer entry to the registry (`mdx-full` → `SandboxedMDXViewer`) and a `trust` prop on `ViewerProps`.

## Shiki bundle size

Default `import("shiki")` → Rollup traces all dynamic imports statically and bundles every grammar and theme. 3+ MB extension. Unacceptable.

Fix: import `shiki/core` + `shiki/engine/javascript` + per-language `shiki/langs/<name>.mjs` explicitly. Rollup code-splits each language into its own lazy chunk. The `shiki/engine/javascript` engine avoids the WASM Oniguruma regex engine (~600 KB). Main bundle drops to ~260 KB gzipped, and the 35 supported languages sit in their own chunks loaded on first render of a block in that language.

Tradeoff: JavaScript regex engine is slightly slower than WASM Oniguruma and drops support for a handful of grammars we don't care about.

## Task list persistence — `remark-gfm` disabled trap

`remark-gfm` hard-codes `disabled` on the `<input>` it emits for task-list checkboxes. DOM-level change events **don't fire on disabled inputs**, so our controlled `TaskCheckbox` never received `onChange` → state never flipped → storage write never happened, even though the input appeared interactive because I'd styled it.

Fix: destructure `disabled` off the props spread in `TaskCheckbox` and drop it on the floor. One line, massive behavioral difference.

## Task index stability

Task checkboxes are identified by their position in the document (0-indexed among all `input[data-fv-task]` in the live DOM). Computed at click time via `document.querySelectorAll(...)` + `indexOf(this)` — not at mount, not via ref callback. Mount-time computation loses because ref callbacks run per-element during commit, and `querySelectorAll` at each call returns an in-progress (shorter) list. Click-time computation is cheap, stable, and correct regardless of which order refs happened to mount in.

Storage key is `fv:task:<fileId>` with a `{ [index]: boolean }` shape. Restoration scans the same index after mount.

Edge case: if the markdown file's task-list structure changes between writes, the indices can desync. Acceptable for v0.1 — a content-hash key would fix but isn't worth the complexity yet.

## `file://` interception without `unsafe-eval`

Chrome MV3 allows content scripts on `file://*` when the user toggles "Allow access to file URLs" on the extension details page. This is a per-extension user toggle; we cannot script around it.

Flow:
1. Content script `content.js` (classic script, no imports, single-line IIFE after Vite's build) runs at `document_end` on every `file://` URL.
2. URL-extension check: `/\.(md|mdx|markdown)(\?[^#]*)?(#.*)?$/i`. Bail early on non-markdown files to keep Chrome's native text-file rendering as the default.
3. Chrome renders local markdown as `text/plain` inside a `<pre>`. Content script reads `document.querySelector("pre").textContent` — that's the entire raw file. No `fetch` call needed (and would be blocked by origin anyway).
4. Stash `{ url, content, name }` into `chrome.storage.session` under a fresh per-request key.
5. Redirect the tab to `chrome.runtime.getURL("src/app/index.html") + "?intercept=" + key`.
6. On the app side, `pickupIntercept()` runs after `hydrate()`, pulls the entry, materializes a one-off file in the library store, sets it active, removes the session key, cleans the URL via `history.replaceState`.

Why `chrome.storage.session` instead of passing content through URL hash? Large markdown files hit URL length limits. Session storage is per-tab-session, auto-garbage-collected when the tab closes, and handles multi-MB payloads fine. Hash-fallback exists for very old Chrome, but modern Chrome always has session storage.

Why `document_end`, not `document_start`? Need Chrome to have already rendered the text into `<pre>`. `document_start` would race the native text-file renderer.

Re-entry guard: `sessionStorage.setItem("fv-handled", url)` before the redirect. Prevents a loop if Chrome for any reason navigates back.

`web_accessible_resources` manifest entry declares `src/app/index.html` + `assets/*` as reachable from `file://`. Without this, Chrome blocks the redirect from file:// → chrome-extension:// as cross-origin.

## Adapter pattern (the portability claim)

`ViewerProps` from `@file-viewer/core`:

```ts
interface ViewerProps {
  content: string;
  file: FileRef;
  storage?: StorageAdapter;
  assets?: AssetResolver;
  onNavigate?: (href: string) => void;
  trust?: "full" | "safe";
}
```

Storage and asset resolution are host responsibilities. The viewer does not import `chrome.*`, `vscode.*`, `fs`, `path`, or any host-specific module. Chrome host wires `IndexedDBStorageAdapter` (via `idb-keyval`) and `FSAAssetResolver` (resolves relative image paths against a `FileSystemDirectoryHandle`, creating blob URLs on demand and caching them). A future VS Code extension will wire `workspace.fs.readFile`-backed adapters. A standalone demo would use `localStorage` + `fetch`.

Enforcement is by convention today. v0.2+ should add either a lint rule (`no-restricted-imports` banning `chrome`, `vscode`, `node:*` inside `packages/**`) or a CI check that rejects PRs touching the packages with those imports. Convention-only contracts fail silently.

## FSA handle persistence

`FileSystemDirectoryHandle` objects can be stored in IndexedDB via `idb-keyval` directly — Chrome serializes them. On page load, `queryPermission({mode: "read"})` tells us whether the previously granted permission still holds. If not, `requestPermission` must be called synchronously in response to a user gesture. So after a fresh Chrome restart, the user clicks "Reconnect folder" on the sidebar → that click provides the user-activation token that lets the permission prompt show.

Handles persist across sessions. Permission grants persist within a session but are re-requested after browser restart. This is a Chrome security constraint, not something our code can bypass.

Session-live file handles (per-file `FileSystemFileHandle` for every renderable file inside a picked folder) are kept in a plain in-memory `Map` (`sessionHandles` singleton). Not serialized because that's cheap to rebuild — one directory walk after reconnect.

## Deferred, intentionally

- **MDX JSX expressions** — need sandboxed iframe. Architecture supports it.
- **JSON / code / CSV / image / log viewers** — each lands as its own package; registry plugs them in.
- **URL interception for remote markdown** (raw.githubusercontent, gist raw, `text/plain`-served `.md` URLs on the open web). Needs content script on `<all_urls>` or `matches` patterns; tradeoff is a broader permission ask.
- **Edit mode** (Monaco or CodeMirror). Deferred to v0.2+.
- **Custom icons** — using `http-lens` placeholders.

## Numbers (gzipped)

- Main app chunk: ~264 KB
- Shiki core: ~32 KB, per-lang: 2–80 KB lazy
- KaTeX CSS: ~30 KB, fonts load as needed
- Content script: single line, ~0.9 KB
- Total cold-load UI ready: under 500 KB

## Install / reload gotchas for future me

- Every `pnpm build` requires a **reload on the `chrome://extensions` card** — Chrome caches extension code between reloads.
- After adding new permissions / matches to the manifest, Chrome forces a reload automatically on next click, but file-URL access toggle **resets** on some Chrome versions. Check it after manifest-permission changes.
- Content scripts can't be loaded as ES modules in MV3 without jumping through hoops — keep `content.js` as classic script with no imports.
- Service worker is a module (`"type": "module"` in manifest). The reload WS plugin relies on that for `import.meta.env.MODE`.

## Files that would break if touched carelessly

- `apps/chrome-ext/vite.config.ts` — the `entryFileNames` function pinning `service-worker.js` and `content.js` to fixed names. Manifest references those by name.
- `apps/chrome-ext/public/manifest.json` `content_scripts.js` and `web_accessible_resources.resources` — changing a filename here without changing the vite config breaks the extension silently.
- `packages/mdx-viewer/src/shiki.ts` — any `import("shiki")` (instead of `shiki/core` + explicit langs) will re-bloat the bundle to 3+ MB.
- `packages/mdx-viewer/src/TaskCheckbox.tsx` — the `disabled` destructure is load-bearing; if reintroduced, task lists silently stop working.
